hot.pointer_line: On now: the clocks went back on 25 Oct, the Virgin tapestries close on 31 Oct, All Saints on Sun 1 Nov and Armistice Day on Wed 11 Nov are public holidays, the 2026 wines are in barrel after an August harvest, Mont d'Or is in the shops, Art in Situ runs to December, and the Trois Glorieuses fill 13–16 Nov with the 166th Hospices sale on Sunday 15 Nov.

groups.title: In the vines and the cellars
groups.desc: The 2026 wines are in barrel after the earliest harvest on record, the houses open their cellars for the auction weekend, and Art in Situ stays out on the Route to December.

items.name: The 2026 wines, new in barrel
items.teaser: Picking began on 13 August in Le Montrachet: the earliest Burgundy harvest in nearly 500 years, per the press
items.story: The 2026 vintage came in fast. Domaine Leflaive began picking its Le Montrachet on Thursday 13 August, ahead of the 1556 benchmark of 15 August, and Vinetur called it Burgundy's earliest harvest in nearly 500 years; the traditional start is early to mid September. Chanson says it began on 19 August in heat and drought that recalled 2003. Leflaive reports high sugars, good acidity and very clean fruit; Chanson and growers on a Beaune forum speak of small berries and lower yields in the Côte de Beaune. No official BIVB report was found. These are the wines the Hospices sell on 15 November.
items.why: Taste a 2026 from barrel this autumn: the same young wine the auction prices in November.
facts: In barrel now; harvest from 13 Aug 2026
Cellars of the Côte de Beaune

items.name: Mont d'Or, back since 10 September
items.teaser: The spruce-boxed Haut-Doubs cheese went on sale on 10 Sept 2026; it is made only 15 Aug to 15 March
items.story: Mont d'Or is not a Burgundian cheese but the winter one Burgundy eats: a soft cow's-milk cheese from the Haut-Doubs, bound in a strip of spruce and sold in a spruce box. The AOP rule makes it a seasonal one. Making starts on 15 August, and the 2026–27 season opened for sale on 10 September 2026; production stops on 15 March and sales run to about mid-May (sources give 10 May or mid-May). The specification was last approved by ministerial order on 18 December 2025. Baked whole in its box, it is a November supper.
items.why: Bake it in its box with a splash of white wine, and serve potatoes and charcuterie alongside.

items.name: The 166th Vente des Vins, Sunday 15 November
items.teaser: The 2026 wines sold under the Halles from 14:30 with Sotheby's; the charity barrel is for rare diseases
items.story: On Sunday 15 November 2026 the Hospices de Beaune sell the 2026 vintage in 228-litre barrels for the 166th time, under the Halles from 14:30, with Sotheby's at the rostrum. Bidding, in the room and online, is open to registered buyers and professionals only. The charity barrel goes to rare diseases: DEBRA France, for people with epidermolysis bullosa, and ARSLA, which works on Charcot's disease. In 2025 the sale made EUR 18.75 million at the hammer, including EUR 400,000 for the charity barrel. The catalogue and order of sale were not published when this was checked.
items.why: Without a paddle, stand outside the Halles for the results, or watch the sale online.

items.name: The harvest on the Côte
items.teaser: Traditionally early to mid September; in 2026 the first grapes came in on 13 August
items.story: The harvest is not a ticketed event but the year's working peak: pickers in the rows from dawn, tractors in the village streets, the cuveries running late. Its date follows the summer. The traditional start is early to mid September, but recent hot years have pulled it earlier; in 2026 Domaine Leflaive picked Le Montrachet from 13 August, which the press called the earliest in nearly 500 years. Cellars are busy and some close to visitors while they work; the fermentations run on into October.
items.why: Visit just after the harvest, in October, when growers have time to talk.
facts: Late August to September, depending on the year

items.story: The Trois Glorieuses are three days built around the Hospices de Beaune sale on the third Sunday of November. The sale and the two dinners are for buyers and guests; the tasting and the street are for everyone.

bougie.title: 1859 — The year the hospital's wine went under the candle
bougie.desc: How a hospital for the poor came to be paid for by its vines, and how the sale of those vines' wine became the most watched auction in Burgundy.
bougie.lede: The Hôtel-Dieu of Beaune, founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin and Guigone de Salins, ran on gifts, and the gifts that lasted were vines. From a first plot in the 1450s the estate grew to about 60 hectares, and since 1859 its new wine has been sold each November, barrel by barrel, to fund the hospital.
paras: Rolin, chancellor to Philip the Good, and his wife founded the hospital in 1443, and patients were nursed in the Hôtel-Dieu from 1452 until 21 April 1971, when the modern hospital opened. Vines came as bequests. Sotheby's and Vinfolio date the first to 1457, a plot called Beaumont-le-Franc from Guillot or Jean Guillotte le Verrier; others give 1459 and Jean Plampays and his wife. The estate now holds about 60 hectares, some 50 of them Pinot Noir (Justerini & Brooks says over 61).

The wine was sold to pay for care. Sotheby's says the Hospices first sold by auction in 1795, then switched between auctions and private sales until 1859, the first of the annual sales; Berry Bros. dates the first auction itself to 1859. The new wine goes young, in 228-litre barrels called pièces, and the buyer raises and bottles it. In 1859 the bidding ran by candle: the last bid before the flame went out took the lot. One account says two candles had to burn down.

For decades négociants did the buying. Christie's took the sale over in 2005, on Sunday 20 November, and for the first time private buyers could bid without a négociant; Christie's ran it to 2020, and Sotheby's won the tender from 2021. The candle survives for the charity barrel. On 16 November 2025 the 165th sale made EUR 18,754,670 at the hammer, the third-best total on record, including EUR 400,000 for a Pommard premier cru Les Rugiens Pièce des Présidents, for EHCO and the Institut Robert-Debré.

_corrections: Old guide: 'free care for 528 years, until 1971'. Patients were nursed in the Hôtel-Dieu from 1 January 1452 to 21 April 1971 (Geneawiki), and the care was only free for the poor; the '528 years from the first gift of vines in 1457' sum does not hold: 1443 to 1971 is 528 years, 1457 to 1971 is 514.

First gift of vines: 1457 (Guillot or Jean Guillotte le Verrier, Beaumont-le-Franc, per Sotheby's and Vinfolio) versus 1459 (Jean Plampays and his wife, per Cavesa and France Travel Planner). Disputed; both given.
First auction: 1859 is the first of the annual series; Sotheby's records an earlier auction in 1795 followed by alternating auctions and private sales.

Candle: Sotheby's says the 1859 sale ran by candle and that the custom still applies to the charity barrel; the year the candle stopped being the rule for every lot was not found. Old guide 'sold by candlelight' for the whole sale is not supported.
2025 charity barrel: EUR 400,000 is confirmed (Pommard 1er cru Les Rugiens, for EHCO and Institut Robert-Debré); the old guide's 'to a Chinese buyer' is not confirmed by any source found.
Estate size: about 60 ha (Vikidia; 85% premier and grand cru per the old guide, not re-verified); Justerini & Brooks says over 61 ha. No dated 2026 figure found.
Christie's ran the sale 2005–2020 (first Christie's sale Sun 20 Nov 2005); Sotheby's since 2021 after a five-year tender.
